Drywall Texture Types, and How to Tell What You Have

A patch that is structurally perfect and texturally wrong still looks like a patch. Here is the vocabulary you need to talk about it.

June 10, 2026 · 6 min read

When people say a repair "looks patched", they are almost never seeing a structural flaw. They are seeing a texture mismatch — a slightly different grain, a slightly different sheen, a rectangle that catches the light at a different angle from the wall around it.

The textures you will actually encounter here

Orange peel

Fine, even stipple, like the skin of an orange. Sprayed on and left alone. Overwhelmingly the most common texture in homes built here from the 1970s onward — the default in San Ramon, Dublin, Brentwood and most of Clayton. Relatively forgiving to match, though the spray pressure and mud consistency have to be right.

Knockdown

Sprayed the same way, then flattened with a wide knife once it has set slightly — producing mottled flat islands with texture between them. Very common on 1980s and 90s construction. The difficulty is timing: knock too early and it smears, too late and it barely flattens. Matching an existing knockdown means matching someone else's timing from thirty years ago.

Skip trowel

Applied by hand with a curved trowel, leaving thin, irregular, sparse patches. Common on 1960s–80s custom homes and around Moraga and Lafayette. There is no machine that does this. It is a hand skill and it has to be matched by hand.

Hand-troweled / Santa Fe / Venetian-look

Broad sweeping trowel marks, sometimes polished, often unique to the person who applied it. Found on older custom homes throughout Lafayette, Orinda and the west side of Walnut Creek. These are matched with sample panels and patience, and sometimes honestly not matched at all — the better answer can be re-finishing the whole wall.

Smooth (Level 5)

No texture at all: a full skim coat, sanded flat, primed. The dominant choice in contemporary remodels. It is the most expensive finish and the least forgiving — under raking light, a smooth wall shows every flaw, and repairs on smooth walls almost always mean re-skimming the whole plane rather than blending a patch.

Older acoustic / popcorn

Ceilings only, mostly pre-1980, and subject to asbestos testing before anyone touches it.

How to identify yours in thirty seconds

  1. Turn off the lights and shine a phone torch along the wall, almost parallel to it. Raking light reveals texture that flat light hides.
  2. Run your palm across it. Fine even bumps is orange peel. Flat plateaus with valleys is knockdown. Sparse raised islands is skip trowel. Broad sweeping ridges is hand-troweled. Nothing at all is smooth.
  3. Photograph it in that raking light. That photo is more useful to a contractor than any description.

Why the sheen matters as much as the grain

Even a perfect texture match can read as a patch, because new compound absorbs paint differently from a wall that has been painted three times. That is what primer is for — and it is why we prime repairs as standard rather than handing over bare mud and hoping the paint sorts it out.

When blending is not the honest answer

On smooth walls, on unusual hand-applied finishes, and on any wall where the light rakes hard across a large flat plane, a blended patch will be visible no matter who does it. In those cases re-texturing the full wall costs more up front and less overall, because it does not have to be redone.

Not sure what you have? Send a raking-light photo and we will name it for you.
